content: 1. Approximately 80% of the global population is at risk of contracting one or more vector-borne diseases. 2. Vector-borne diseases account for 17% of the global burden of communicable diseases. 3. Annually, over 700,000 deaths are attributed to vector-borne diseases. 4. Vectors such as mosquitoes, flies, bugs, and others transmit viruses, parasites, and bacteria that infect millions of people worldwide. 5. These vectors are responsible for diseases such as malaria, dengue, leishmaniasis, Chagas disease, and Zika virus disease. 6. The World Health Organization (WHO) has developed a new strategy to enhance global vector control efforts. 7. Member States endorsed this integrated approach during the 2017 World Health Assembly and adopted a resolution to support the strategy. 8. Specific vectors and their associated diseases include: Flies: onchocerciasis, human African trypanosomiasis. Ticks: Lyme disease, Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever, tick-borne encephalitis, typhus. Fleas: murine typhus, plague. Mites and lice: rickettsialpox, typhus. Snails: schistosomiasis. Triatomine bugs: Chagas disease. Mosquitoes: chikungunya, dengue, Japanese encephalitis, lymphatic filariasis, malaria, yellow fever, Zika virus disease, Rift Valley fever, West Nile fever. 9. In recent years, vector-borne diseases have expanded into new territories, with diseases previously confined to tropical and subtropical regions now increasingly appearing in temperate areas. 10. Vector-borne diseases continue to cause outbreaks and persistent health challenges across all WHO regions. 11. The WHO strategy aims to reduce the burden and threat of vector-borne diseases through effective, locally adapted, and sustainable vector control measures. 12. Success depends on countries' ability to realign and strengthen their vector control and surveillance programs with adequate staffing and financial resources. 13. National strategic plans must be revised, and country-specific targets defined to achieve these goals. 14. Vector-borne diseases disproportionately affect impoverished populations, exacerbating poverty and hindering development by interfering with education and work capacity. 15. These diseases also have significant economic impacts, such as reducing tourism opportunities in affected regions. 16. The Global Vector Control Response 2017–2030 aligns with the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and contributes to achieving Goals 1, 3, 6, 11, 13, and 17. 17. The strategy emphasizes integrated and locally adapted vector control, which is cost-effective, with an estimated global annual cost of $330 million, or about 5 cents per person at risk. 18. This cost includes strengthening the workforce, coordination, and surveillance capacity, with allocations of 33% for vector surveillance, 24% for coordination and planning, and 43% for staff and training. 19. The strategy sets milestones and targets to reduce mortality and case incidence of vector-borne diseases globally by 30% and 25%, respectively, by 2020; 50% and 45% by 2025; and 75% and 60% by 2030, relative to 2016 levels. 20. It also aims to prevent epidemics of vector-borne diseases in all countries without transmission in 2016 and ensure rapid detection and containment of outbreaks to prevent cross-border spread. 21. Key actions include increasing capacity, improving surveillance, and better coordinating and integrating efforts across sectors and diseases. 22. Enabling factors for success include strong country leadership, advocacy, resource mobilization, partner coordination, regulatory and policy support, and community engagement. 23. Communities must be empowered to lead and sustain vector control activities, such as eliminating vector habitats and improving housing conditions. 24. The number of public health entomologists worldwide must be increased, and appropriate field and laboratory capacity must be ensured to strengthen vector surveillance and control. 25. Research on innovative solutions must be aggressively pursued to build a strong evidence base for effective interventions. 26. National surveillance systems for vectors, interventions, and diseases must be strengthened and integrated. 27. Vector control methods must be tailored and combined appropriately for local settings, with innovations integrated as recommended by WHO. 28. Comprehensive vector control focuses on prevention by targeting vectors, which is the most effective approach for most vector-borne diseases. 29. Millions of people have already benefited from vector control, with significant reductions in diseases such as malaria, Chagas disease, and onchocerciasis. 30. However, vector control has not been fully utilized or sustained to maximize its impact on other diseases.
